label: Temple Scroll 11Q19 (Megillat HaMikdash) — Part 3 — Col 45–66
summary_plain: The final section of the Temple Scroll covers the purity of the Temple city, laws of vows and oaths, regulations for witnesses, laws of warfare, and the statutes for the entire land of Yisra’el. The Temple city itself is holy — no impurity may enter it. The scroll details what may and may not be brought into the city. Laws about idolatry are strict: if a city worships other gods, it shall be utterly destroyed. The warfare regulations prescribe how Yisra’el shall go to battle: the priest shall speak to the army, and YHWH shall fight for them. The scroll concludes with a comprehensive restatement of the covenant blessings and curses.
summary_scholarly: Columns 45-66 of the Temple Scroll cover the purity of the Temple city (expanding on Devarim’s laws of the camp), laws of vows and oaths (paralleling Bamidbar 30), laws of witnesses (expanding Devarim 17:6-7 and 19:15), laws of warfare (rewriting Devarim 20), and the apostasy laws (expanding Devarim 13). The scroll treats the entire Temple city as a sacred zone equivalent to the wilderness camp of Yisra’el, applying the purity laws of Bamidbar and Vayikra to urban space. The warfare regulations require priestly involvement in military decisions, consistent with the War Scroll (1QM). The apostasy laws are more detailed than the Masoretic Torah. The final columns effectively create a comprehensive legal code for the ideal covenant society — a constitution derived entirely from Torah rewritten as YHWH’s direct speech.

key_terms.definition: Columns 56-59 of the Temple Scroll contain detailed laws governing the king — selection, marriage, military, economic, and judicial rules. The king must be chosen by YHWH, must be from among the covenant brothers, may not multiply horses or wives, and must write a copy of the Torah before him every day of his life.

The Temple Scroll's king requirement: the king must have a scroll of this Torah written for him by the priests and Levites, and read in it every day of his life so that he may learn to revere YHWH and not exalt himself above his brothers. This is Devarim 17:18-20 expanded into law.

The Temple Scroll's king may not multiply wives for himself. Specifically, he may not take a wife from outside the people of Yisra'el, and he may not take a second wife as long as the first lives — a stricter standard than mainstream practice.

The Temple Scroll specifies that 1,000 men are the king's permanent guard — not an unlimited army, but a specifically limited personal guard. The community's king is a servant of the covenant, not a monarch accumulating power.

The Temple Scroll's Part 3 opens with detailed purity regulations: who may enter the Temple city, how skin disease, bodily discharge, and death-impurity are handled, and the requirement for a three-day purification period for certain impurities before entering the Temple area.

Columns 64-66 of the Temple Scroll include laws about capital crimes — those who betray the people to a foreign nation or who flee to a foreign nation to bring an army against Yisra'el. These traitors are to be hanged on a tree.

The Temple Scroll cols 64-66 expand on Devarim 21:22-23 — a person guilty of treason (betraying Yisra'el to a foreign nation) is to be executed and hanged on a tree. This is a judicial execution method for the most serious political crimes, not associated in this context with the NT's later application.

The Temple Scroll describes a judicial system with judges appointed in every town, a supreme court for difficult cases, and the king bound by the same laws as the people. The judicial system is covenant-based, not royal decree.

The Temple Scroll specifies that the military camp must maintain high purity — provisions for latrines outside the camp, covering bodily waste, maintaining the camp's ritual cleanliness during warfare. These rules echo Devarim 23:12-14 but are elaborated.

The Temple Scroll's king is fully bound by the covenant — he may not exalt himself above his brothers, may not multiply silver and gold, may not accumulate military power beyond the specified guard. The covenant constrains the king as it constrains everyone. The king is not above the Torah.

faq.question: What are the Statutes of the King in the Temple Scroll?
faq.answer: Columns 56-59 of the Temple Scroll contain detailed laws about the ideal covenant king: he must be chosen by YHWH from among the covenant brothers, may not be a foreigner, may not multiply wives (not while the first lives), may not accumulate excessive horses, silver, or gold, must have a Torah copy written for him and read it daily, and may not exalt himself above his brothers. His permanent guard is 1,000 men. These laws are an expansion of Devarim 17:14-20, made into binding covenant statute.

faq.question: What is the significance of the king's daily Torah reading requirement?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll requires the king to have a Torah copy written for him by the priests and Levites, and to read in it every day of his life 'so that he may learn to revere YHWH and not exalt his heart above his brothers.' This daily requirement means Torah is not just the king's constitutional constraint — it is his daily formation. The king who reads the Torah every day is a king shaped by covenant values, not just bound by covenant rules. The Temple Scroll envisions a king formed by the Torah from the inside, not merely restrained by it from the outside.

faq.question: What does the marriage law tell us about the Temple Scroll's ethics?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll's king may take only one wife, and may not take a second while the first lives. This is stricter than the mainstream Tanakh record (Dawid had multiple wives; Shlomoh had hundreds). The Temple Scroll applies a monogamy standard to the king that the community also applied to community members in the Damascus Document (CD prohibits taking a second wife while the first lives). This reflects a consistent covenant-law position: marriage is a covenant bond that cannot be multiplied or dissolved while the first partner lives.

faq.question: What crimes does the Temple Scroll consider capital offenses?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll includes treason among capital crimes: someone who betrays Yisra'el to a foreign nation, or who flees to a foreign nation and brings an army against Yisra'el, is to be executed and hanged on a tree. This expands the Devarim 21:22-23 provision (which covers someone guilty of a sin worthy of death) to cover specifically political treason. The community understood the covenant's survival as requiring the most serious penalty for those who endangered it by siding with foreign powers.

faq.question: What is the 'hanging on a tree' in the Temple Scroll?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll cols 64-66 expand Devarim 21:22-23 to cover treason: political traitors who betray Yisra'el to a foreign nation are to be executed and hanged on a tree. This is a judicial punishment for the most serious political crime — not a sacrificial or religious execution, but a civic punishment for covenant betrayal. The same passage (Devarim 21:22-23) is later applied by Paul in Galatians 3:13 in a completely different theological framework. The Temple Scroll's application is straightforwardly judicial: treason carries the death penalty and public display.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll constrain royal power?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll's king is structurally limited: he may not multiply wives, horses, silver, or gold; his permanent guard is specifically 1,000 men; he must read the Torah daily to remain formed by covenant values; he may not exalt himself above his brothers; and he is chosen by YHWH, not by his own lineage or dynastic succession alone. The covenant is the king's constitutional frame — he is as bound by it as the smallest member of the community. This is a radical anti-monarchic theology embedded in the structure of the community's ideal kingdom.

faq.question: How do the purity laws of Temple Scroll Part 3 work?
faq.answer: The purity laws (cols 45-51) define who may enter the Temple city zone and under what conditions. Certain impurities require a three-day waiting and purification period before entry. The laws cover skin disease, bodily discharge, and death-impurity. The Temple city (the broader sacred zone, not just the Temple mount) is maintained at a higher purity standard than the rest of Yerushalayim. The laws ensure that the entire sacred geography around YHWH's dwelling is maintained at covenant purity — not just the innermost courts.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll's judicial system ensure covenant accountability?
faq.answer: Judges are appointed in every town to handle local disputes. Difficult cases go to a supreme court. The king himself is judged by the same Torah laws as everyone else — there is no royal exception. The judicial system is not the king's instrument of power but the covenant's mechanism for holding everyone accountable, including the king. This consistent accountability is what distinguishes the Temple Scroll's covenant kingdom from the kind of monarchy that the Prophets critiqued — where kings used courts to protect their own interests.

faq.question: What do the military camp purity laws mean for the community's warfare theology?
faq.answer: The military camp must be maintained at the same purity standard as the community's covenant life — latrines outside the camp, bodily waste covered, no impurity within the camp. This is because YHWH is present in the camp ('for YHWH your Creator walks in the midst of your camp' — echoing Devarim 23:14). Warfare is not a suspension of covenant life; it is covenant life under different conditions. The camp is as sacred as the Temple city in the sense that YHWH's presence is there — that presence demands the same purity discipline.

faq.question: How does Temple Scroll Part 3 complete the scroll's theological vision?
faq.answer: Parts 1-3 together present a complete covenant society organized around YHWH's presence: Part 1 establishes the sacred architecture; Part 2 establishes the covenant calendar and festival cycle; Part 3 establishes the purity laws, judicial system, and royal accountability that govern the people's life within that sacred space and time. Together they describe a society where every dimension — space, time, law, and leadership — is ordered by YHWH's covenant. It is the most comprehensive blueprint for a covenant society in the entire DSS corpus.
